p5: Good evening, investors and analysts. Thank you very much for attending our 2026 interim results briefing. I will first give a brief introduction to Zhipu’s basic situation, our recent thinking, and our future technology roadmap.
p6: Large-model technology has been developing for nearly ten years. Since last year, Zhipu has recognized that large models are shifting from “chatting” to “doing,” and we positioned ourselves for this transition relatively early, with a particular focus on strengthening our models’ coding capabilities. In the middle of last year, we released GLM-4.5, our first model to achieve strong results in coding. Since the beginning of this year, we have successively released GLM-5.0, 5.1, 5.2, and 5.3, all of which have continued to iterate on the same foundation.
p7: First, does scaling necessarily mean substantially increasing the number of parameters? Scaling is a key path toward higher intelligence, but its essence is not simply expanding parameter count. Since the beginning of this year, we have significantly strengthened the scale of the base model, post-training, and task environments. While expanding parameter scale, it is also necessary to increase the model’s effective depth：for example, by using a Loop Transformer to allow the model to think more deeply during inference. We have recently been advancing related work. At the same time, there remains substantial room for improvement in post-training. We therefore invested heavily in GLM-5.3 and significantly strengthened its post-training.
p8: Coding also encompasses many different types of tasks. Strengthening the model across a range of coding tasks can systematically improve its overall capabilities. We did a great deal of work on different task environments, which significantly improved GLM-5.3’s performance and brought it to a SOTA level and the current frontier of intelligence.
p9: On the other hand, a model must not only be powerful; users must also be able to afford and access it. When designing a model, we need to consider model size and active parameters, as well as inference and infrastructure efficiency. Only by reducing inference costs can the technology be made broadly accessible.
p10: For this reason, when designing the GLM-5 series, we placed particular emphasis on strengthening inference capabilities. In a computing environment where Nvidia chips coexist with a variety of domestic Chinese chips, we drew on external resources and acquired an inference-technology company to further strengthen our inference capabilities, making GLM-5.1, 5.2, and 5.3 easier to deploy and use.
p11: Current model usage is substantial, and our usage volume on OpenRouter at one point ranked first. After each new model release, call volume on our MaaS platform has generally doubled. That is a basic overview of our overall positioning and progress this year.
p12: For a model R&D company, the core task remains continuously pushing up the frontier of intelligence. This brings us back to Zhipu’s most fundamental vision. In 2019, we set a single vision for Zhipu: to make machines think like humans. To this day, we are still exploring the upper bound of intelligence. Exploring that upper bound is not only about training models; it also requires us to think about what kind of intelligence future models should possess and what they should be able to accomplish. We have developed several lines of thought around the next stage of our roadmap.
p13: First, at the beginning of this year, we saw that coding had become a direction broadly recognized by the industry. We then thought further about how models could accomplish more tasks on top of their coding capabilities. Around GLM-5.1 and 5.2, we proposed the concept of the Long Horizon Task, hoping that models could execute longer-horizon tasks; we also proposed Autonomous AI, meaning that a model should be able to complete a task autonomously.
p14: Once models possess these capabilities, they will still need to evolve further. We have already begun research into fully self-training models. We hope models will be able to autonomously learn through pre-training, mid-training, and post-training, and autonomously build their own harnesses, so that the training process gradually becomes autonomous.
p15: You may have noticed that in our recent inference optimizations：especially during the release of GLM-5.3 and the optimization of infrastructure for domestic chips：we have already been using an Infra Agent. The Infra Agent powered by GLM-5.3 can autonomously revise optimization plans for domestic chips, significantly improving results. In the future, we will continue along this path and further strengthen these capabilities.
p16: Finally, as we work to make AI more broadly accessible and usable by more people, social responsibility is equally important. The release and large-scale use of models require robust governance and safety mechanisms. We continue to consider how to strengthen models’ capabilities in social governance, public safety, and ethics, and we have already begun related research. We also hope investors and analysts will offer more suggestions and support as we jointly explore the frontier of AGI and the path toward broadly accessible AI.
p17: Next, I will give a comprehensive report on our achievements and thinking in the first half of the year. In summary, if last year’s keyword was the “intelligence frontier,” then the keyword for the first half of this year was “turning capability into value.” For the first time, models have been proven to be not merely tools, but systems capable of independently completing a task. Our revenue structure changed accordingly, and the commercial value of strong models began to be realized at scale.
p18: The first section concerns our thinking on strategic focus and model development. First, the intelligence frontier determines the task boundary, while task value determines the commercial opportunity. At our annual results briefing in March, we proposed a formula:
p19: AGI commercial value = intelligence frontier × scale of token consumption
p20: The intelligence frontier determines what tasks a model can handle and how much user value each token can create. The higher the intelligence frontier, the higher the value density of the tasks the model can process, and the greater the economic output corresponding to each unit of intelligence. The scale of token consumption reflects the breadth and depth with which intelligence is being used. The same token, when used for casual conversation versus repairing a vulnerability in a production environment, may generate outcomes differing by several orders of magnitude. The value density of the scenario in which a token is used therefore depends on the task boundary the model is able to open up. Each time that task boundary rises by one level, the market opportunity may expand by an order of magnitude.
p21: Our second point concerns the five stages of model-capability development. We believe the evolution of large-model capabilities is not a set of parallel product lines, but a staircase that progresses in sequence:
p22: Chat → Coding → Agent → Cowork → Autonomous AI
p23: Chat delivers a one-off answer. Coding delivers executable code. Agent delivers a completed multi-step chain of tasks. Cowork delivers work products that can be reviewed by professionals.
p24: Autonomous AI delivers the capability to operate continuously. Each step upward has a specific technical threshold. Unless that threshold is crossed, the business model at the next level cannot be established. From Chat to Coding, the threshold is whether the result can be verified. From Coding to Agent, the threshold is long-horizon planning and error recovery. From Agent to Cowork, the threshold is whether reliability is high enough that professionals are willing to review the result rather than rebuild it from scratch. From Cowork to Autonomous AI, the threshold is whether the model can autonomously determine whether its result is correct. During the reporting period, the company’s focus was between Coding and Cowork. We have already begun experiments in cybersecurity, legal services, finance, education, and other fields. Cybersecurity has progressed the fastest; the other directions remain at an early stage and have not yet generated revenue at scale.
p25: Our models achieved a score of 84.5 on CyberGym, surpassing Fable5 and GPT-5.6 SOLO. On ExploitGym, they completed 130 tasks, second only to Fable5 and GPT-5.6.
p26: Our third point is the importance of maintaining a continuously improving model-iteration trajectory and SOTA-level performance. Over the past year, the industry’s understanding of SOTA has been changing. Short-term leadership on a leaderboard is no longer the most important thing. What truly matters is who can continuously bring stronger models to market at a faster pace and at a better cost. A single-point championship is fleeting; sustained excellence is a trajectory that keeps moving upward.
p27: The GLM series completed six iterations in approximately eleven months. Its intelligence index rose from 32 to 60, while cost per task remained around the US$0.20 level. GLM-5.3 Flash entered the intelligence-cost frontier with a cost per task of US$0.045. With coding as its entry point, GLM-5 opened up long-horizon intelligence. Its capabilities expanded from code generation to system understanding, task planning, tool use, and engineering interaction, pushing models from vibe coding toward agentic engineering. Programming has become the company’s main source of revenue, and the long-horizon task capabilities accumulated through coding have also been validated through transfer to fields such as cybersecurity.
p28: GLM-5.2 is a flagship model for long-horizon tasks. It supports a genuinely usable 1M-token context window and, in practice, can accommodate project-level engineering context. It is more stable in long-horizon task execution and more reliable in following engineering conventions. Its success rate in development scenarios has improved further, and it can complete an entire development chain：from requirements to deployable outputs across multiple endpoints：in a single task.
p29: GLM-5.3 is Zhipu’s latest flagship model, with comprehensive advances in complex software engineering and Agent tasks. It uses the same base model as GLM-5.2, and all of its capability gains came from post-training. GLM-5.3 further scaled up its task environments, so that training tasks were no longer limited to conventional programming problems but more closely resembled complete units of professional work performed by experts in real-world settings. With the same architecture, the same total parameter count, and the same number of active parameters, merely expanding the scale of post-training improved end-to-end completion rates by more than 50%. GLM-5.3 demonstrates that scaling is not only about parameters; training is currently the area with the greatest room for improvement.
p30: If GLM-5.3 represents the current capability frontier, then GLM-5.3 Flash represents the cost frontier. Designed for high-frequency, large-scale, cost-sensitive usage, GLM-5.3 Flash uses a new architecture developed specifically to reduce costs. It has 320 billion total parameters and 18 billion active parameters, combines sparse attention with linear attention, and is priced at one-tenth the level of GLM-5.2. Its performance in both benchmarks and real-world applications is superior to GLM-5.2.
p31: Before release, the model was tested under the anonymous model names OX and Aux Offer through real-world usage on OpenCode and OpenRouter. On its first day online, it ranked first on OpenRouter and set a new record for single-day token usage. Total usage over six days exceeded 62 trillion tokens, driving overall platform usage up by more than 20%.
p32: Our fourth point is progress in “using domestic chips to power domestic models.” Since the beginning of the year, we have incorporated domestic Chinese chips into our primary inference capacity. GLM-5.3 Flash is the company’s first model to provide services entirely through domestic-chip clusters under ultra-large-scale, real-world traffic. The chips are connected through our self-developed high-bandwidth interconnect network, and the entire inference engine was substantially accelerated by an Infer Agent powered by GLM-5.3, cutting operator-development cycles in half. For the first time within the company, we have completed the loop in which “the model optimizes the system, and the system runs the model.”
p33: Compared with the initial baseline on the same hardware, end-to-end service performance improved threefold. The company has achieved large-scale, low-cost inference on approximately 100,000 domestic accelerator cards, and inference cost per token has fallen by 80% compared with the beginning of the year. Against a backdrop of persistently tight global compute supply, this path means we have begun to take control of our own cost curve.
p34: Next, Xiao Lei will introduce the company’s financial data.
p35: Good evening, investors. I will now introduce the company’s financial performance and business development.
p36: In the first half of 2026, total revenue reached RMB 954 million, equivalent to US$142 million, representing year-on-year growth of nearly 400%. More noteworthy than the growth rate itself was the shift in revenue composition. Revenue from the open platform and API business reached RMB 825 million, equivalent to US$123 million, more than 27 times the level of the first half of last year. Its share of total revenue rose sharply from 15.2% in the same period last year and 26.3% at the end of last year to 86.5%. Zhipu’s revenue is now generated primarily by the open platform and API business. The recent releases of GLM-5.2, GLM-5.3, and GLM-5.3 Flash drove a historic surge in open-platform and API business volume.
p37: As of the end of August 2026, our ARR had reached US$1.6 billion. This ARR is calculated by annualizing monthly revenue：that is, by multiplying August revenue by twelve. Frontier-model companies overseas and some companies in the industry also use a more aggressive method, multiplying the latest week’s data by 52. Taking the ramp-up of GLM-5.3 into account, ARR under that method has already exceeded US$2 billion.
p38: More important than the ARR figure itself are the drivers behind it. Since the beginning of the year, Zhipu has achieved relatively healthy growth in both volume and price. As of the end of August, token usage on the MaaS platform had increased by more than 40 times compared with the beginning of the year, including growth of more than 23 times for CodingPlan. Average API pricing rose by approximately 101%. This indicates that the historic surge in platform revenue was driven mainly by model capability rather than relying entirely on price elasticity.
p39: Benefiting from both higher volume and higher pricing, gross margin also improved substantially. Gross margin for the open-platform and API business rose from negative 0.4% in the first half of last year to 24.6% in the first half of this year：an improvement of 25 percentage points year on year and approximately six percentage points from the 18.9% recorded for last year as a whole.
